about.title: Fire and Evacuation Plans for Someone Who Uses a Wheelchair or Cannot Walk
about.length_note: About 14 minutes: 16 short beats, one idea each. You can stop after any beat and pick up again. The topics (exits, helpers, being trapped, carries, practice) each need their own step, so this class sits near the top of the 5 to 15 minute range.

say.text: Welcome to class nine. Today you will draw a home fire escape plan that works for someone who uses a wheelchair or cannot walk. You can stop after any step.

show.text: A fire escape plan built around the person

say.text: One promise first. This is planning help. It does not replace a first-aid class, the person's own doctors, or advice from your local fire department.

show.text: Check with your local fire department

say.text: Why plan ahead at all? The Red Cross says you may have less than two minutes to get out of a burning home.

show.text: Less than 2 minutes

ask.q: The Red Cross says about how long you may have to escape a burning home?
wrong: About ten minutes
About half an hour
As long as you need
ask.why: Fire can spread fast, so the plan has to be made before a fire, not during one.

say.text: First idea: two ways out of each room, where possible. If fire blocks one way, you use the other.

show.text: Two ways out of each room

say.text: Here is an example. Sam uses a wheelchair. Sam's bedroom has a door to the hall and a patio door. A way out only counts if Sam can really get through it.

show.text: A simple floor plan: Sam's bedroom with a hall door and a patio door, each marked with an arrow

ask.q: How do you test whether the patio door counts as a second way out for Sam?
ask.right: Check that Sam can get through it in the wheelchair
wrong: Assume any door counts
Count it even if a couch always blocks it
Count it without anyone ever trying it
ask.why: The U.S. Fire Administration advises people who use a wheelchair or walker to check every exit to be sure they get through the doorway.

say.text: Second idea: where the bedroom is. The U.S. Fire Administration says that in a multistory home, sleep on the first floor. Being on the ground floor and near an exit makes escape easier.

show.text: Ground floor, near an exit

ask.q: Which bedroom spot makes escape easier, according to the U.S. Fire Administration?
ask.right: On the ground floor, near an exit
wrong: Upstairs, as far from the door as possible
In the room farthest from every exit
It makes no difference
ask.why: Being on the ground floor and near an exit makes escape easier. If you cannot move rooms, the rest of this class still helps.

say.text: Home changes can help too, such as exit ramps and wider doorways. Keep furniture from blocking a quick exit.

show.text: Exit ramps | Wider doorways | Furniture out of the way

say.text: Now draw it. NFPA has a free escape grid. Draw the floor plan, show all doors and windows, and mark two ways out of every room.

show.text: A grid page with rooms, doors and windows, and two coloured arrows leaving each room

say.text: The Red Cross map also has a meeting spot outside. You need one so you know everyone in the home is out.

show.text: Floor plan with a red path to the front yard and a star for the meeting spot

say.text: Third idea: who helps. If someone cannot escape alone, name a helper in the household. Name a backup too, in case the helper is not home.

show.text: Helper | Backup

ask.right: The first helper might not be home when the fire starts
wrong: Because one helper is never enough for any plan
So nobody has to practise
So the plan can skip the meeting spot
ask.why: The fire department and NFPA both suggest a backup in case the first person is away.

say.text: Pick a meeting spot at a safe distance, such as a neighbour's home or a specific tree. Once everyone is out, call 911. Never go back inside for people, pets or things.

show.text: Get out | Stay out | Call 911 from outside

ask.q: If everyone can get out, when do you call 911?
ask.right: Once you are out, at the meeting spot
wrong: After going back for valuables
After searching every room again
Only after the fire is out
ask.why: The Red Cross says to get out and then dial 911, and never to go back inside.

say.text: What if someone cannot get out, because smoke or fire blocks the way? NFPA says to close all doors between you and the fire. A closed door may slow smoke, heat and fire.

show.text: Close the doors

say.text: The Red Cross adds a warning. Do not open a door that feels warm to the back of your hand. Use another way out instead.

show.text: Warm door? Use a second way out.

say.text: Then call the fire department, even if someone has already reported the fire. Say exactly where you are trapped. If you can, wave a flashlight or light-coloured cloth at the window.

show.text: Close doors | Call and say exactly where | Signal at the window

ask.q: You are trapped in a back bedroom. What should you tell the call-taker?
ask.right: Your address, the exact room and side of the house, and that you cannot leave
wrong: Just the word 'help'
Only that there is a fire
Nothing, because someone else already called
ask.why: Firefighters need to know exactly where you are, even if someone else has already reported the fire.

say.text: To make that call possible, sleep near a phone. Keep a working flashlight in the sleeping area. If the person cannot speak, the helper outside can give the room and window. Write both on your map.

show.text: Phone within reach | Flashlight by the bed | Room and window written on the map

say.text: In larger buildings you may hear 'area of refuge'. It is a space that serves as a temporary haven from fire. In your own home, a safe room to wait in is something to talk through with your fire department.

show.text: Area of refuge

say.text: Now a safety line. Do not try lifts or carries down stairs without training. NFPA says people who need assisted rescue should talk with the fire department about how they will be carried so they are not injured. An occupational therapist can help you plan this too.

show.text: Ask first. Do not improvise a carry.

ask.q: No one in the home is trained to carry Sam down stairs. What is the safest plan?
ask.right: Talk with the fire department or an occupational therapist before a fire
wrong: Practise a carry on your own at night
Decide on the day of the fire
Never tell anyone about the plan
ask.why: Carries can injure the person being moved, so the method is worked out with trained people in advance.

say.text: Tell your local fire department the plan. Many departments take non-emergency calls. Explain the needs, and they may suggest escape ideas and look at your home. Services vary, so check with your local fire department.

show.text: Call the non-emergency line | Describe who lives here and what they need | Ask for advice on your own home

say.text: Last step: practise. NFPA says to practise twice a year and make the drill as realistic as possible. Practise at different times of day. Time it, to learn what to improve. Do not treat the time as a pass or fail.

show.text: 2 drills a year

say.text: Practise again whenever the plan changes. A new chair, a new bedroom or a new helper all count. FEMA and the Red Cross say to practise as often as you update your plan.

show.text: Draw the plan, practise, change something, update the plan, practise again

ask.q: Besides twice a year, when should you practise again?
ask.right: Whenever you update the plan, for example after a change in equipment or helpers
wrong: Only if a fire happens
Never, once the map is drawn
Only when the fire department visits
ask.why: FEMA and the Red Cross say to practise as often as you update your escape plan.

say.text: To finish, here is your checklist: two ways out of each room, a ground-floor bedroom if you can, clear exits, helper and backup, a meeting spot, a phone and flashlight, advice on carries, a call to the fire department, and drills. Well done.

show.text: Two ways out | Ground floor | Clear exits | Helper and backup | Meeting spot | Phone and flashlight | No untrained carries | Tell the fire department | Practise twice a year

notes.topic: Power cuts and equipment that must travel

other_side.claim: A safe room or area of refuge to wait for firefighters can be part of the plan.
other_side.other_view: BrainLine reports that many fire chiefs support areas of refuge. It also reports that, since September 11, many people with disabilities have been reluctant to rely on them and want to leave with everyone else. NFPA's guide says waiting with the person for first responders would likely be a last choice when there is an imminent threat. Talk it through with your fire department. This is why the class treats it as a backup idea.

other_side.claim: Trained helpers or evacuation devices can carry a person down stairs.
other_side.other_view: NFPA says such devices and carries need trained people and a talk with the fire department. Fire-service guidance from Northern Ireland (UK, so local rules may differ) warns that carry-down methods put some people at risk of injury. It says every carry-down method needs a risk assessment. So experts agree on training and advance planning, not on one best method.
